GRCop-84 is a high conductivity, high strength copper alloy developed by NASA Glenn for use in high temperature, high heat flux applications such as rocket motor combustion chamber liners and nozzle ramps.

Metallic coatings like NiCrAlY and Cu-8-30%Cr have shown promise in improving the performance of GRCop-84 by prohibiting blanching, reducing 'dog-house' failures, increasing operating temperatures, and decreasing cooling requirements.
Microsample specimens were prepared from extruded, 40 mil cross-rolled, and 20 mil cross-rolled GRCop-84 using wire EDM, lapping, and plunge EDM with graphite electrodes.

The microsample tensile tests showed 12-14% strain to failure, in good agreement with NASA's macroscale results, and revealed the expected trends of increased strength and decreased ductility with increased cold/warm work from rolling.
JHU will test microsample specimens of plasma sprayed Cu-26Cr and NiCrAlY coatings in both as-deposited and thermally cycled conditions, measuring RT and 600°C tensile properties.
Bond strength tests will be conducted with the GRCop-84/coating interface oriented perpendicular and at 45° to the tensile axis for different surface conditions and thermal cycling states.

JHU can conduct elevated temperature (600°C) microsample tensile and creep tests by resistively heating the specimens, using a two-color infrared pyrometer to measure the temperature with 1°C resolution and verifying temperature gradients less than 5°C.
NASA has provided plasma sprayed monolithic coatings of Cu-8Cr, Cu-26Cr, NiCrAlY and NiAl, as well as overlay coatings of NiCrAlY and Cu-XCr (X=8-56) on GRCop-84 substrates for JHU to test.

The microsample testing approach allows measurement of highly scale-specific properties that complement conventional macroscale testing, providing critical data for modeling and optimization of the coating-substrate system.

In addition to tensile and stress relaxation tests on the coatings, JHU will conduct out-of-plane bond strength tests with the GRCop-84/coating interface oriented perpendicular and at 45° to the tensile axis.
The microsample testing has been successfully used by JHU to characterize a wide range of materials at small scales, including thin films, coatings, and microstructural features.
The integration of microsample testing with detailed microstructural observations provides a mechanistic foundation for coating optimization and life prediction modeling.

The overall objective is to elucidate and model the thermal stability and mechanical integrity of candidate coatings for the GRCop-84 copper alloy, which has potential applications in high temperature, high heat flux components of reusable launch vehicles.
The key tasks include NASA depositing candidate coatings, JHU conducting microsample testing and microstructural characterization, and incorporating the data into FE-based life cycle models.
The microsample tensile and stress relaxation tests will allow JHU to measure the small-scale, highly specific properties of the as-deposited and thermally cycled coatings.
